findings.headline: The council refinanced long-term market loans in February 2026, generating a £1.597m fair-value credit to fund reserves.
findings.detail: The council restructured long-term market loans in February 2026, resulting in a £1.597m credit to CIES from reduction in fair value of the loans. After interest adjustments, this enabled a transfer of £1.143m to reserves. This active refinancing during the year, while beneficial, suggests the council was actively seeking ways to manage debt and bolster its reserve position.
findings.matters: Loan restructuring can indicate proactive debt management, but using fair-value gains on refinanced debt to fund operational reserves and ongoing deficits masks underlying cash generation problems. It shows the council is using non-operating gains to sustain its financial position.
findings.figures: Fair-value credit £1.597m; transfer to reserves £1.143m; total borrowing £180.2m (down from £183.4m); weighted average interest rate 3.41%
findings.quote: The restructuring of two long term market loans in February 2026 resulted in a credit to CIES of £1.597 million arising from the reduction in the fair value of the loans. After interest adjustments associated with the restructure, this enabled a transfer to reserves of £1.143 million.

findings.headline: The Square asset useful life has been reduced to 25 years with a depreciation method change, triggering a £1.933m additional revenue provision charge.
findings.detail: The council's asset valuation (carried out by CBRE for 2025/26 accounts purposes) significantly reduced the useful life of The Square asset to 25 years and changed the depreciation method from annuity to straight line, because the asset is no longer classified as investment property. This triggered a voluntary revenue provision (MRP) charge of £1.933m. The S151 officer describes this as 'prudent' and notes it was only affordable due to interest savings elsewhere.
findings.matters: A sudden reduction in an asset's useful life and reclassification away from investment property suggests concerns about the asset's performance, cash-generative ability, or long-term viability. This may signal underlying operational or market pressures on a key council property.
findings.figures: Useful life reduced to 25 years; voluntary revenue provision charge £1.933m; change from annuity to straight-line depreciation
findings.quote: A voluntary revenue provision of £1.933 million has been included in the outturn as a result of the useful life of The Square being reduced to 25 years in the most recent valuation from CBRE, and a change in method to straight line from annuity as the asset is not being classed as investment property.

findings.headline: Capital programme severely underspent: only £5.346m spent against £17.474m budgeted (69% slippage).
findings.detail: The council budgeted to spend £17.474m on capital in 2025/26, but actual outturn was £5.346m. Even Q3 projection of £7.886m was exceeded by the final underspend. A total of £11.077m is to be reprofiled into future years (£8.86m already reported at Q3, plus a further £2.217m identified at year-end), with £1.055m of budgets released entirely.
findings.matters: Repeated significant capital slippage suggests poor forecasting, planning difficulties, or constrained project delivery capacity. This affects the council's ability to maintain assets and execute planned service improvements.
findings.figures: Original capital budget £11.739m; revised budget £17.474m; outturn £5.346m; Q3 projection £7.886m; total reprofiling £11.077m; releases £1.055m
findings.quote: The outturn was £5.346 million, significantly below that budgeted, and below that reported at quarter 3 of £7.886 million.

findings.headline: General usable reserves fell 32% in one year, from £17.207m to £11.408m.
findings.detail: The council's general earmarked reserves (discretionary funds available to spend) fell by £5.799m during 2025/26, alongside a further £1.312m movement in specific reserves. Total usable reserves closed at £20.927m from an opening balance of £25.414m. At this depletion rate, general reserves could be depleted within 5-6 years.
findings.matters: Reserves are a buffer against unexpected costs and income shortfalls. Rapid depletion signals the council is consuming its contingency, leaving little room for adverse events or revenue pressures.
findings.figures: Opening general reserves £17.207m; closing £11.408m; net movement £5.799m reduction; total usable reserves closed £20.927m
findings.quote: The updated balance of reserves is shown below: Specific £9.519m, General £11.408m, Total £20.927m

findings.headline: The council requires £4.063 million from reserves to balance the revenue budget, and the S151 officer states this is unsustainable.
findings.detail: The council's normal operations generate a deficit: net cost of services £17.209m against funding received of £13.146m. This £4.063m gap is filled from reserves. The S151 officer explicitly states 'the use of reserves to fund ongoing revenue expenditure is unsustainable in the medium to long term' and notes the council will 'enter West Surrey Council with an annual deficit being funded by reserves.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if a council can sustain debt service from operations, not from one-off reserves drawdowns. An ongoing structural deficit is a material credit risk.
findings.figures: Use of reserves £4.063m; net cost of services £17.209m; funding received £13.146m
findings.quote: Whilst the use of reserves to fund ongoing revenue expenditure is unsustainable in the medium to long term, we embarked on a transformation programme and the changes we have made as a result, are shown in the under spend in the outturn report. These will not, however, return the Council to a position where it does not rely on reserves to balance the budget, and will enter West Surrey Council with an annual deficit being funded by reserves.

findings.headline: Property portfolio vacancy increased materially, with retail at 10% and industrial at 7% by estimated rental value
findings.detail: Retail vacancy at The Square climbed to 10% by estimated rental value (from 6% a year earlier), reflecting structural market challenges. Office and industrial vacancy rose to 7% by ERV from 4% in the prior year, with Theta property maintaining a persistent 16-17% vacancy. Rising vacancies reduce the rental income base at a time when the council's property investments are already delivering barely sufficient coverage of interest costs.
findings.matters: Continued vacancy increases will further erode property income. With investment cover ratio already at 1.02x, material vacancy growth could cause property income to fall below interest expense, requiring the council to service debt from reserves or restrict other spending.
findings.figures: The Square retail vacancy 10% by ERV (March 2026) vs 6% (March 2025); office/industrial total 7% by ERV vs 4%; Theta property 17% vacancy

findings.headline: The Square retail property had useful life cut to 25 years, requiring £1.933m accelerated depreciation provision
findings.detail: CBRE's recent valuation of The Square reduced its useful life to 25 years, triggering a £1.933m voluntary revenue provision for accelerated depreciation. The council justified this as a 'prudent approach' but the decision signals that a major asset is deteriorating faster than previously assumed. Vacancy at The Square increased to 10% by estimated rental value, up from 6% a year earlier. The council was only able to absorb this charge due to the one-off £1.143m benefit from loan restructuring.
findings.matters: Material write-down of a major asset signals concerns about its physical condition or market prospects. The asset deterioration was masked in prior years and only surfaced when professional valuation was done. If other assets similarly need revaluation, further provisions may follow.
findings.figures: Useful life reduced to 25 years; voluntary revenue provision £1.933m; The Square vacancy 10% by ERV (March 2026), up from 6% (March 2025)
findings.quote: A voluntary revenue provision of £1.933 million has also been included in the outturn as a result of the useful life of The Square being reduced to 25 years in the most recent valuation from CBRE... and the revised asset life was based on the age, specification and anticipated capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Surrey Heath BC External Audit Plan 25-26
findings.headline: 14 audit recommendations from prior years (2023/24 and 2024/25) remain unresolved and tracked for follow-up
findings.detail: The audit plan appendix tracks 14 audit recommendations from the prior two years, with follow-up status to be reported in the 2025/26 audit findings report (scheduled November 2026). The auditors have introduced a formal escalation policy for audit delays, suggesting prior implementation of recommendations has been slow and may have contributed to prior-year audit completion issues.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit recommendations indicate control weaknesses have not been remediated. Slow closure of audit findings is associated with repeated failures and systemic control gaps.
findings.figures: 14 audit recommendations from 23/24 and 24/25; follow-up report due November 2026
findings.quote: As we reported the status of these findings and management's responses in our 24/25 Audit Findings Report in February 2026, we will carry out follow-up work as part of the 2025/26 audit. We will report on the Council's progress in implementing these recommendations in our 25/26 Audit Findings Report scheduled for November 2026.

findings.paper_title: Surrey Heath BC External Audit Plan 25-26
findings.headline: Independent review identified control weaknesses in £9m annual property rental income stream
findings.detail: The council receives approximately £9m annually from property investments and uses managing agencies to administer them. The council's own independent review identified weaknesses in these arrangements. The audit plan flags a risk that sufficient progress is not being made to remediate the weaknesses.
findings.matters: A £9m income stream with known control weaknesses and third-party administration creates risk of income loss, misappropriation, or management bypass. This is roughly 16% of gross operating costs.
findings.figures: £9m annual property rental income; independent review identified weaknesses
findings.quote: The Council has approximately £9m rental income from property and uses managing agencies. The Council's independent review of property arrangements identified weaknesses in arrangements. There is a risk that sufficient progress is not being made to improve the arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Surrey Heath BC External Audit Plan 25-26
findings.headline: Pension liability increased more than fourfold to £8.9m, driven by assumption changes
findings.detail: The council's net pension liability moved from £2m in 2023/24 to £8.9m at 31 March 2025. Auditors confirm the calculation methodology is routine, but flag that the estimate is highly sensitive to small changes in key assumptions around discount rates, inflation, salaries, and life expectancy. This is identified as a significant risk requiring specialist audit procedures.
findings.matters: A material balance sheet movement of this scale reduces net assets and indicates obligation size was materially mis-stated in prior year. Further movements are possible if economic assumptions shift.
findings.figures: Pension liability 23/24: £2m; 31 March 2025: £8.9m
findings.quote: The Council's net Pension liability at the end of 31st March 2025 was £8.9m (23/24, Pension liability £2m). Small changes in key assumptions (discount rate, inflation rate, salary increase and life expectancy) can have a significant impact on the estimated IAS 19 asset.

findings.paper_title: Surrey Heath BC External Audit Plan 25-26
findings.headline: £27m structural budget gap in medium-term financial strategy, addressed only by reserve depletion and undelivered transformation savings
findings.detail: The audit plan identifies a significant weakness in the council's arrangements for financial sustainability. The medium-term financial strategy shows a £27m funding gap over 2026/27 to 2029/30. Management has stated its transformation programme alone cannot bridge the gap, meaning reserves will be drawn down annually. There is explicit risk the transformation programme does not deliver planned savings, further depleting reserves.
findings.matters: A structural deficit dependent on reserve drawdown means the council has no financial flexibility for unexpected pressures or new borrowing, and faces immediate stress once reserves are exhausted.
findings.figures: £27m gap in MTFS 2026/27–2029/30; annual reserve drawdown; budget sustainability dependent on undelivered transformation programme
findings.quote: The medium term financial strategy covering 2026/27 to 2029/30 highlights a gap of £27m. It is acknowledged that its Transformation programme alone cannot bridge annual gaps and reserves will be utilised. There is a risk the Council's Transformation programme does not yield planned savings increasing the demand on reserve balances.

findings.paper_title: Surrey Heath BC External Audit Plan 25-26
findings.headline: No audit opinion issued for 2024/25, and no assurance available over opening balances for 2025/26
findings.detail: A disclaimer of opinion was issued on the 2024/25 financial statements due to the audit backstop deadline. For 2025/26, the auditors have no assurance over opening balances and will focus only on in-year transactions and closing balances capable of standalone verification. This follows five years of disclaimed audits.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot rely on audited financial statements when no audit opinion exists. Without assurance over opening balances, year-on-year financial movement analysis is unreliable and the council's true position is unknown.
findings.figures: Prior 5 set of accounts disclaimed; 2024/25 disclaimer issued; 2025/26 opening balances to be unaudited
findings.quote: In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025, a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the backstop. We will have no assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26. We will work with the Council to rebuild assurance over time.

findings.headline: Internal audit function was significantly understaffed for nine months due to vacancies and sector-wide recruitment challenges.
findings.detail: The council's in-house audit team operated at reduced capacity due to vacancies for nine months (April–December 2025), prompting a switch to the Southern Internal Audit Partnership from 1 January 2026. While the chief internal auditor concluded this did not materially impair the audit opinion, it represents a period of governance weakness in the control environment and audit coverage.
findings.matters: A functioning internal audit function is a cornerstone of governance assurance for lenders. Extended understaffing signals governance fragility and reduces the likelihood of identifying emerging financial or operational problems in real time.
findings.figures: Nine months of reduced coverage (April–December 2025); transition to external provider from 1 January 2026
findings.quote: Due to a number of vacancies within the internal audit service and challenges nationally in recruiting to the profession, alternative delivery options were explored. From 1 January 2026 Surrey Heath Borough Council joined the Southern Internal Audit Partnership for the future provision of their internal audit service.

findings.headline: External asset management review identified seven critical governance and financial reporting weaknesses requiring remediation.
findings.detail: Local Partnerships LLP conducted an independent review of the council's physical asset management practices and rated the council at 'aware' to 'developing' maturity levels (below competent). Seven findings were rated critical, including gaps in the Master Asset Register, asset categorisation, financial reporting requirements, procurement compliance, and the governance and assurance framework. An action plan to address these recommendations was presented to the Performance and Finance Scrutiny Committee on 15 April 2026.
findings.matters: Lenders assess borrowing capacity partly on asset quality and governance over procurement and financial reporting. Critical weaknesses in asset register accuracy, categorisation, and financial reporting controls could mask liabilities or inflate asset values, materially affecting credit decisions.
findings.figures: Seven critical recommendations; Council rated at Level 1 (aware) to Level 2 (developing) on Institute of Asset Management maturity scale
findings.quote: Seven are rated critical and relate to Master Asset Register enhancements, asset categorisation, current Service-level priorities, financial reporting requirements, procurement compliance, governance and assurance framework and strategic asset management planning.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating staff retention and capacity risks through April 2027 transition
findings.detail: The council identifies managing LGR workload alongside business-as-usual delivery with reduced headcount as an anticipated issue for 2026/27, with particular risk to staff retention and corporate knowledge transfer to the new West Surrey Council following vesting day in April 2027.
findings.matters: Key staff losses during major transition could disrupt critical finance, planning, and service functions; knowledge loss affects ongoing service delivery and transition execution quality
findings.figures: No specific turnover numbers or headcount reductions quantified
findings.quote: LGR additional workload of supporting implementation while keeping BAU running effectively, with reduced head count. In addition to the need to end/close down well and hand over to new authority. Loss of corporate knowledge into new authority.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation provision at risk as planning permission expires June 2027
findings.detail: Housing Resettlement service is managing ongoing engagement with a Registered Provider for temporary accommodation, ahead of a June 2027 planning expiry and planned redevelopment of existing units. This creates a potential gap in service provision.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation pressure is a leading indicator of homelessness costs; loss of provision without replacement would push costs to emergency services and nightly-paid temporary accommodation, increasing budget unpredictability
findings.figures: No figures on number of units or current usage
findings.quote: Continue engagement with the Registered Provider to secure future temporary accommodation provision, ahead of the June 2027 planning expiry and redevelopment of existing units.

findings.headline: Prior-year disclaimed audit opinion with outstanding issues on property accounting and debtors
findings.detail: The council has unresolved governance weaknesses from the 2024/25 audit, specifically a disclaimed audit opinion relating to accounting treatments for property managing agents, property accounting, and debtor/creditor balances. These are being worked through in the current year.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinion means auditors could not form a view on financial statement accuracy; unresolved property and debtor accounting issues indicate potential control weaknesses affecting the reliability of the balance sheet
findings.figures: No figures given; nature of the issues (property accounting, debtor/creditor balances) suggests potentially material items
findings.quote: To review accounting treatments for property managing agents under agency/principal rules and addressing outstanding issues following the 2024/25 disclaimed audit opinion, particularly in relation to property accounting and debtor/creditor balances.

findings.headline: Planning application income decline creating budget gap in Development Management
findings.detail: Development Management service identified a budget gap arising specifically from reduced planning application income. The service is addressing this through vacancy savings and income promotion measures including Planning Performance Agreements.
findings.matters: Planning fees are discretionary council income; decline suggests economic weakness in the local development market or loss of market share, affecting predictable revenue
findings.figures: No quantified figures for the income gap or scale of reduction
findings.quote: Key improvements will address the planning budget gap arising from reduced application income by maintaining vacancy savings, promoting the use of Planning Performance Agreements, and strengthening budget monitoring through regular reviews of actual and forecast income.

findings.headline: Council using reserves to balance budget, with acknowledged long-term sustainability risk
findings.detail: The council has reduced in-year funding and has been using financial reserves to balance its budget. The statement acknowledges that reserves cannot be replenished once spent and that continued reliance on this approach represents a significant risk unless future budgets can be balanced between expenditure and funding.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion indicates structural budget pressures and limited headroom for unexpected costs or further funding cuts; material for assessing repayment capacity and budget sustainability
findings.figures: No specific figures given for reserve levels or planned depletion rates
findings.quote: With the ongoing reduction of in-year funding the Council has had to use some of its financial reserves to help balance its budget. Reserves can only be drawn on once and when spent are unlikely to be replenished; continual use of reserves to balance the budget represents a significant risk in the long term unless future budgets are balanced between expenditure and funding.

findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer limits his confidence statement to 2026/27 only; states medium-term position requires 'corrective action soon'
findings.detail: The S151 Officer explicitly states confidence is limited to the 2026/27 budget only, and that 'the adequacy of reserves is not sufficient over the medium term'. He identifies that 'further mitigating actions' are required 'soon' and notes the position 'is no longer sustainable'.
findings.matters: The S151 Officer is the statutory authority on financial robustness; limiting confidence to one year signals the council is beyond normal management and approaching insolvency
findings.figures: Confidence limited to 2026/27; reserves negative in 2027/28
findings.quote: the Council's Chief Finance Officer (Section 151 Officer) is confident that the estimates of expenditure and income are robust for 2026/27 budget only, and the adequacy of reserves is not sufficient over the medium term

findings.headline: Debt financing costs rising to 87.86% of net revenue by 2029/30, leaving inadequate headroom for service delivery
findings.detail: The Prudential Indicators show the ratio of net financing costs to net revenue rising from 54.82% in 2026/27 to 87.86% by 2029/30. With interest costs themselves rising from £6.12m to £8.25m annually, debt service consumes nearly 88% of revenue by 2029/30.
findings.matters: A council spending 88% of revenue on debt interest cannot deliver services; this signals over-leverage during a period of structural deficit
findings.quote: Ratio of net financing costs to net revenue stream 54.82% 69.35% 79.39% 87.86%

findings.headline: Rental income loss of £1.086-1.244 million is structural and accounts for 48-60% of budget growth
findings.detail: The S151 Officer identifies that loss of rental income on property is the primary driver of budget growth, representing 48% of the £2.4m growth in 2026/27 and rising to 60% by 2028/29. This indicates systematic underperformance of the council's property portfolio.
findings.matters: Rental income loss of this scale indicates asset quality or occupancy issues in the council's property portfolio; this is structural revenue decline, not temporary
findings.figures: £1.086m rental income loss 2026/27; £1.244m by 2028/29; represents 48-60% of total budget growth
findings.quote: Of the £2.4 million growth, 48% in 2026/27 relates to loss of rental income (£1.086 million). This rises to 60% by 2028/29 (£1.244 million).

findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £8-9 million per annum that the S151 Officer explicitly states is unsustainable
findings.detail: The S151 Officer states the transformation programme alone 'will not be enough to bring the MTFS forward budgets back into equilibrium'. The £8-9m annual deficit represents 43-48% of the £18.84m budget and has persisted despite £5.1m in savings over recent years.
findings.matters: A structural deficit this large cannot be closed by incremental transformation; it signals fundamental economic imbalance requiring strategic intervention
findings.figures: Budget gap £8-9m per annum on £18.84m budget; £5.1m savings achieved in recent years overwhelmed by £3.3m growth in last two budget rounds
findings.quote: the budget gap in future years has risen to between £8 million and £9 million per annum. This level of growth is not sustainable.

findings.headline: Reserves projected to reach negative position in 2027/28, indicating structural insolvency
findings.detail: The S151 Officer explicitly states that whilst reserves are adequate for 2026/27, current expenditure projections will result in a negative reserve position during 2027/28, directly impacting the new West Surrey Council. This forces a choice between exceptional financial support, service cuts, or asset disposals.
findings.matters: A council with negative reserves cannot pay liabilities; this is an insolvency trigger requiring government intervention or service abandonment
findings.figures: Reserves negative in 2027/28; £2.3m drawn from earmarked reserves in 2026/27
findings.quote: current expenditure projections over the MTFS period show the level of reserves dropping below a level deemed to sufficient to cover unknown risks and contingencies, to a negative position in 2027/28 financial year

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation risk: if Lawrence Lodge closes, alternative provision could cost up to £900k per year
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes temporary accommodation needs will be met by Lawrence Lodge (council-owned housing). However, the budget notes that 'if Lawrence Lodge becomes unavailable (as is expected), alternative accommodation will need to be sourced.' Private nightly-paid temporary accommodation costs over £100 per night; housing current occupancy through this route could cost up to £900k annually. This cost is NOT included in the budget because the council believes alternative provision will be found 'with sufficient certainty.'
findings.matters: This is a binary risk: either alternative provision is found (no additional cost), or it is not and costs explode by £900k in a single year. Given reserve depletion, a £900k unexpected cost would breach the general fund balance and force emergency intervention.
findings.figures: Current temporary accommodation cost assumption: £0; potential cost if Lawrence Lodge unavailable: up to £900k per year (100+ nights @ £100+/night)
findings.quote: If Lawrence lodge becomes unavailable (as is expected), alternative accommodation will need to be found. Temporary accommodation can cost over £100 a night. Housing the current occupancy of Lawrence lodge through this option could cost up to £900,000 per financial year.

findings.headline: General Fund Balance of £538k is below prudent minimum and would be exhausted by a single emergency
findings.detail: The general fund balance is currently only £538k, which falls below the prudent minimum of 5–10% of net budget (£1m–£1.8m). The council acknowledges this and states 'it is prudent to increase this to £1 million.' However, the reserve drawdown strategy makes it unlikely that this prudent level will be achieved, leaving the council dangerously undercushioned against unexpected events.
findings.matters: A general fund balance of £538k provides almost no buffer against service disruption, emergency costs, or forecast error. This increases financial fragility and indicates the council is operating at the edge of viability.
findings.figures: Current general fund balance £538k; prudent level £1m–£1.8m (5%–10% of net budget); 2026/27 forecast to remain at £538k
findings.quote: The level of the General Fund Balance is currently £538,000, and forecast to remain at that level, and is excluded from the above table, it is prudent to increase this to £1 million in line with the policy of keeping 5% to 10% for contingencies.

findings.headline: Revenue account subsidising property portfolio due to interest costs exceeding net rental income
findings.detail: The council has a deficit of rental income over council-wide financing costs. Net property operating income is £5.865m (2026/27), but interest payable is £6.1m, meaning the revenue account is subsidising the property investment portfolio. The council acknowledges 'the revenue account is subsiding the property portfolio and capital investments due to the higher interest costs, although they do have an economic benefit to the taxpayer.'
findings.matters: Property acquisitions are now a drag on the revenue budget rather than an investment that pays for itself. This is a sign that the capital strategy is misaligned with the financial position and may require reversal of property strategy.
findings.figures: Net property operating income 2026/27: £5.865m (Commercial £3.575m + Office £621k + Retail £1.669m); interest payable £6.1m
findings.quote: for next year the Council has a deficit of income over Council wide financing costs meaning the revenue account is subsiding the property portfolio and capital investments due to the higher interest costs, although they do have an economic benefit to the taxpayer.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing of £76m and need to access further £20m before 31 March 2026 creates refinancing and interest rate risk
findings.detail: The council has £170m external borrowing outstanding, of which £76m is short-term borrowing. It expects to need up to a further £20m of short-term debt before 31 March 2026 to cover internal borrowing for the capital programme. Short-term rates are budgeted at 3.98% for 2026/27, but there is explicit risk that rates will not decrease as assumed. Interest payable is £6.1m (2026/27), with £4.12m relating to short-term debt.
findings.matters: £76m of short-term borrowing must be rolled over or refinanced annually. If interest rates do not fall as expected, interest costs will exceed budget, forcing further reserve draws or service cuts. This is a material refinancing risk.
findings.figures: External borrowing £170m (£76m short-term); anticipated additional short-term debt £20m before 31/3/2026; interest payable 2026/27 £6.1m (£4.12m from short-term debt); short-term rate 3.98%
findings.quote: In order to fund the previous Council's property acquisition actions, the Council has taken out a significant amount of external borrowing, which currently stands at £170 million, where £76 million is short-term borrowing. It is anticipated that before 31 March 2026, the Council need to access up to a further £20 million of short-term debt.

findings.headline: Transformation savings programme underdelivering; items 'not achievable' or 'lower than anticipated'
findings.detail: The council budgeted £3m base budget savings from transformation and service delivery reviews (2025/26), but reports in section 12.1(e) that 'as we progressed with implementing the transformation programme, there were some items that were subsequently deemed not achievable or achieved lower than anticipated.' The 2026/27 budget includes £562k for 'transformation not achieved' across the MTFS period, acknowledging slippage.
findings.matters: Transformation savings are the only lever to close the budget gap. Slippage here compounds the structural reserve drawdown problem. Service managers' ability to deliver further savings is in doubt.
findings.figures: Transformation not achieved: £562k per year (2026/27–2028/29); this offsets against £3m claimed savings
findings.quote: As we progressed with implementing the transformation programme, there were some items that were subsequently deemed not achievable or achieved lower than anticipated. Services identified other mitigating transformation savings, but as these are progressed there is a risk they may not be achieved as included in the budget.

findings.headline: Retail property portfolio decline driving £1.085m recurring budget pressure from reduced rent income
findings.detail: Tenant insolvencies and new vacancies in 2025/26 (Poundland, River Island, Trilogy, British Heart Foundation) cost £760k in lost income, outstripping new lettings (£489k). Lease renewals at lower market rates cost a further £370k. The council budgets £1.085m reduction in rental income for 2026/27 with no recovery assumed; structural retail sector decline means this risk is ongoing.
findings.matters: Property income is relied upon to service £170m of borrowing. Declining retail valuations and rent are a known tail risk if demand decreases further, which would force either additional reserve draws or service cuts.
findings.figures: Growth item due to reduced net rental income: £885k–£1.085m; tenant insolvencies £760k; lease renewals at lower rates £370k
findings.quote: In practice, tenant insolvencies and new vacancies (£760,000) which included Poundland, River Island, Trilogy nightclub and British Heart Foundation outstripped new income from lettings (£489,000).

findings.headline: Significant reduction in government funding (22.3% excluding council tax over three-year settlement)
findings.detail: Surrey Heath will see a 22.3% reduction in core funding excluding council tax rises over the 2026–2029 settlement period. The FFR (Fair Funding Review) itself results in a reduction of 28.92% overall funding, or £1.3 million over the three years. This is due to the deprivation index weighting and the council's relatively strong tax base.
findings.matters: A 22% funding cut is severe and explains the need for reserve drawdown. This is structural, not cyclical, and will persist into West Surrey Council's baseline.
findings.figures: 0.9% increase including council tax; 22.3% reduction excluding council tax over 3 years; FFR reduction of 28.92% = £1.3m over 3 years
findings.quote: Surrey Heath itself is an increase of 0.9% including council tax, and a reduction of 22.3% excluding council tax. The FFR itself sees a reduction of 28.92% overall funding for Surrey Heath, or £1.3 million over the 3 years.

findings.headline: Council would need Exceptional Financial Support from government for 2027/28 onwards without local government reorganisation
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges that absent the Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) merger into West Surrey Council, it would be applying for Exceptional Financial Support from government to achieve a balanced budget from 2027/28 onwards. This signals the underlying position is not recoverable through transformation and savings alone.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support is a marker of financial distress and comes with significant government conditions. The council's baseline financial position is only sustainable because of the LGR transaction, not because of operational recovery.
findings.figures: Budget gap of £8m–£9m per year from 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: Had it not been for Local Government Reorganisation (LGR), the Council would be needing to ask for Exceptional Financial Support for 2027/28 and beyond and would be working with the Government in achieving a balanced budget.

findings.headline: Reserves depleting to deficit and unsustainable drawdown pattern across MTFS period
findings.detail: General earmarked reserves fall from £6.997m (2025/26) to negative £20.829m by 2029/30. The council explicitly states it is 'budgeting for and projecting to drawdown on reserves over the MTFS period to prepare a balanced budget – this is not sustainable.' Annual movement shows accelerating draws: £2.4m, £7.6m, £9.2m, and £8.1m per year.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion of this scale signals that the council cannot sustain operations without permanent service reduction or income increases. Negative reserves are unsustainable and would require intervention.
findings.figures: Total reserves: 2025/26 £16.644m → 2029/30 (£10.609m); general earmarked reserves fall to (£20.829m) by 2029/30
findings.quote: The Council is budgeting for and is projecting to drawdown on reserves over the MTFS period to prepare a balanced budget – this is not sustainable.

findings.headline: The council's ability to fund new capital programmes depends heavily on realising £8.458m of projected asset sales over the MTFS period.
findings.detail: The council assumes it will sell assets to raise capital receipts of £1.4m (2025/26), £1.748m (2026/27), £1.5m (2027/28) and £3.8m (2028/29). It plans to use £7.048m of these to fund the capital programme. If receipts fall short, the underlying borrowing requirement rises immediately.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the capital programme is actually fundable from receipts or whether it is dependent on optimistic asset sale assumptions. The council flags this: 'If they are not achieved the Council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes will be higher in the earlier years.'
findings.figures: Total estimated capital receipts £8.458m; capital receipts assumed to fund £7.048m of the £8.267m net new capital spend; if not achieved, CFR increases immediately
findings.quote: If they are not achieved the Council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes will be higher in the earlier years.

findings.headline: The council has high leverage: debt is 80% of assets today and will remain 76% by 2029/30, despite a strong asset base.
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges 'we have high gearing despite the strong asset base, as this is predominately funded by borrowing.' The CFR (unfinanced capital) will increase from £198.7m to £207.7m. The council plans to increase underlying borrowing need by £16.36m over the MTFS period.
findings.matters: High leverage limits the council's capacity to absorb further borrowing, asset write-downs, or revenue volatility. Lenders need to assess whether the council can service the planned increase.
findings.figures: Total debt £185.3m (2024/25) rising to £201.3m (2028/29); debt ratio 80% (2024/25) declining only to 76% by 2029/30; CFR increasing from £198.7m to £207.7m in 2026/27
findings.quote: This shows we have high gearing despite the strong asset base, as this is predominately funded by borrowing.

findings.headline: The council's financial constraints force it to limit capital spending to only mandatory and health-and-safety work.
findings.detail: The capital strategy states that 'given the financial health of the Council' it will focus on mandatory and H&S schemes and asset preservation, not discretionary investment. This signals the council has limited room for growth or improvement projects and must prioritise immediate liabilities.
findings.matters: A lender assessing long-term viability needs to know whether the council can invest in modernisation and growth, or whether it is purely in preservation mode. This council appears to be the latter.
findings.figures: 7 new capital bids submitted with net cost of £8.267m over MTFS period; capital contingency held at £200k annually
findings.quote: Given the financial health of the Council, the strategy is to ensure capital expenditure is spent on mandatory and health and safety schemes and work to prevent further deterioration of the Council assets

findings.headline: Investment property rental income has fallen £1.5m annually and the council holds difficult-to-liquidate assets worth £95.1m.
findings.detail: The council's property portfolio earned £9.9m in 2024/25 but is budgeted at only £8.4m for 2025/26 and £8.2-8.4m thereafter. The portfolio is 37% of all long-term assets but the council notes property 'can take a considerable amount of time to sell in certain market conditions.' If market conditions deteriorate further, rents or valuations could fall, hitting both revenue and capital.
findings.matters: Property-dependent income that declines without obvious reason, combined with illiquidity, creates refinancing risk if the council needs to raise cash quickly.
findings.figures: Investment property valued at £95.1m; rent receipts fell from £9.9m (2024/25) to £8.4m projected (2025/26); budgeted at £8.2-8.4m from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: Projected outturn for rental receipts for 2025/26 is £8.4 million.

findings.headline: Financing costs will consume nearly 88% of the council's net revenue stream by 2029/30, leaving little for service delivery.
findings.detail: The proportion of net revenue budget needed to cover interest, MRP and other financing costs for past capital borrowing rises from 54.82% in 2026/27 to 87.86% in 2029/30. This is driven by the council's accumulated debt and rising MRP provisions. The council explicitly warns this is a 'very high proportion' that constrains financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know how much of the council's income is already committed to debt service, as this reduces capacity to absorb new borrowing costs or revenue shocks.
findings.figures: Financing costs rise from £8.7m (54.82% of net revenue stream) in 2026/27 to £12.2m (87.86%) in 2029/30; net revenue stream is £15.8m in 2026/27 but only £13.8m by 2029/30
findings.quote: A very high proportion of the Council's net revenue stream is being used to fund the financing implications of past capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Moratorium on non-essential spend and Finance Control Panel to be imposed in 2026/27 as precursor to possible external intervention
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer recommends implementing a moratorium on non-essential spend 'as a precursor to any external intervention' by central government. A Finance Control Panel will be established; all credit cards will be centralised under exception-only control; all expenditure decisions will go through central review. This step signals expectation that central government intervention may be necessary if the financial position deteriorates further.
findings.matters: A spending moratorium is a precursor to section 114 notice territory; it indicates the council expects the need for external intervention or exceptional support from central government.
findings.figures: Finance Control Panel and moratorium on non-essential spend for 2026/27
findings.quote: As a precursor to any external intervention it would be anticipated by central government that the Council would impose a moratorium on non-essential spend. This is normally controlled by the senior management of the Council (under direction from the Chief Finance Officer)

findings.headline: Council Tax is identified as the only reliable income stream; all other sources are volatile or declining
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly states: 'Of all the income streams the Council has, Council Tax is least volatile and most reliable, therefore is the only one that can provide a stable funding base for services.' The council is increasing Council Tax by the maximum 2.99% without triggering a referendum. However, central government's Fair Funding Review has already reduced assumed funding over the three-year period, mitigated only by a funding floor.
findings.matters: Concentration on Council Tax as the only reliable revenue source means the council has limited flexibility to raise additional income; it is locked into a model where services must decline as costs rise.
findings.figures: Council Tax increase 2.99% (maximum permitted); funding reduction from Fair Funding Review
findings.quote: Of all the income streams the Council has, Council Tax is least volatile and most reliable, therefore is the only one that can provide a stable funding base for services.

findings.headline: Drawing down £2.3 million from earmarked reserves in 2026/27 to balance the revenue budget
findings.detail: The executive recommendation includes approval to draw 'up to £2.3 million' from earmarked reserves to support the revenue budget in 2026/27. This use of reserves to bridge the operating gap is framed by the CFO as unsustainable if continued; each year of drawdown accelerates the path to negative balances.
findings.matters: Relying on reserve drawdown to balance current spending means the council is not self-sustaining; each £2–3m drawdown shortens the runway to insolvency by one year.
findings.figures: £2.3 million drawdown from earmarked reserves
findings.quote: to approve the recommendation by the Head of Finance (the Council's Section 151 Officer) that up to £2.3 million be drawn down from earmarked reserves to support the revenue budget in 2026/27

findings.headline: Transformation programme is explicitly insufficient to prevent budget deterioration alone
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer states: 'with the inflationary pressures and interest charges now baked into the base costs, the transformation programme alone, in its purest form, will not be enough to bring the MTFS forward budgets back into equilibrium, nor protect the sustainability of reserve balances.' Having achieved £5.1m in savings, the council faces £3.3m in new budget pressures (2025/26 and 2026/27), which have erased the savings' benefit.
findings.matters: If the council's primary cost-reduction programme cannot solve the structural problem, more severe measures (reserve depletion, service cuts, asset sales, or central government intervention) are inevitable.
findings.figures: £5.1m savings achieved; £3.3m budget pressures in 2025/26–2026/27
findings.quote: with the inflationary pressures and interest charges now baked into the base costs, the transformation programme alone, in its purest form, will not be enough to bring the MTFS forward budgets back into equilibrium, nor protect the sustainability of reserve balances

findings.headline: Debt financing costs rising to 87.86% of net revenue stream by 2029/30 from 54.82% in 2026/27
findings.detail: The prudential indicator for net financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream escalates from 54.82% in 2026/27 to 69.35% (2027/28), 79.39% (2028/29), and 87.86% (2029/30). Absolute debt interest costs rise from £6.12m to £8.25m. The capital programme commits £26m gross spending with £19m net to be funded by borrowing, which the CFO notes 'will put strain on the Council's debt burden.'
findings.matters: A financing costs ratio approaching 90% of revenue indicates unsustainable debt; this leaves minimal headroom for shocks and constrains the council's ability to deliver services or meet unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Financing costs ratio: 54.82% → 87.86%; debt interest £6.12m → £8.25m; £19m net capital borrowing required
findings.quote: Ratio of net financing costs to net revenue stream 54.82% 2026/27 Proposed, 69.35% 2027/28, 79.39% 2028/29, 87.86% 2029/30

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer provides qualified assurance: robust for 2026/27 only, reserves inadequate medium-term
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly states: 'the Council's Chief Finance Officer (Section 151 Officer) is confident that the estimates of expenditure and income are robust for 2026/27 budget only, and the adequacy of reserves is not sufficient over the medium term.' This is a formal, qualified opinion: assurance is limited to the first year, with explicit recognition that reserve adequacy fails from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: The responsible finance officer is not giving assurance beyond the current year; this formal qualified statement signals to lenders and central government that the council cannot self-correct and will require intervention or restructuring.
findings.figures: Confidence limited to 2026/27; medium-term reserves insufficient
findings.quote: the Council's Chief Finance Officer (Section 151 Officer) is confident that the estimates of expenditure and income are robust for 2026/27 budget only, and the adequacy of reserves is not sufficient over the medium term.

findings.headline: Loss of property rental income is 48% of budget growth in 2026/27, rising to 60% by 2028/29
findings.detail: Of the £2.41m budget growth in 2026/27, the CFO identifies that 48% (£1.086m) stems from loss of rental income on property holdings. This exposure worsens: by 2028/29, loss of rental income accounts for 60% of growth (£1.244m). The CFO specifically flags this as 'the risk the Council has in some of its services, mainly income generation around rental income on property.'
findings.matters: Concentrated exposure to property rental income creates vulnerability to market downturns and refinancing costs; this is a material revenue volatility that affects debt service capacity.
findings.figures: £1.086m rental income loss in 2026/27 (48% of growth); £1.244m by 2028/29 (60% of growth)
findings.quote: Of the £2.4 million growth, 48% in 2026/27 relates to loss of rental income (£1.086 million). This rises to 60% by 2028/29 (£1.244 million).

findings.headline: Structural budget gap of £8–9 million annually is identified as unsustainable
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer calculates that savings from the transformation programme (£5.1m achieved) have been fully offset by budget pressures totalling £3.3m over the last two rounds. With reduced rental income now embedded in the base budget, 'the budget gap in future years has risen to between £8 million and £9 million per annum.' The CFO explicitly describes this as unsustainable without further major action.
findings.matters: An annual deficit of this magnitude means the council cannot achieve balance through efficiency improvements alone and will require either service cuts, asset sales, or external intervention.
findings.figures: Budget gap £8–9 million per annum
findings.quote: the budget gap in future years has risen to between £8 million and £9 million per annum. This level of growth is not sustainable.

findings.headline: Reserves forecast to reach negative position in 2027/28, triggering impact on new West Surrey Council
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer states that while the council has adequate reserves for 2026/27, expenditure projections show 'the level of reserves dropping below a level deemed to sufficient to cover unknown risks and contingencies, to a negative position in 2027/28 financial year.' This will 'directly impact the new West Surrey Council' following local government reorganisation. The transformation programme alone cannot prevent this outcome.
findings.matters: Negative reserves mean the council cannot absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, and signals acute financial distress requiring central government intervention or exceptional support.
findings.figures: Reserves forecast negative in 2027/28
findings.quote: current expenditure projections over the MTFS period show the level of reserves dropping below a level deemed to sufficient to cover unknown risks and contingencies, to a negative position in 2027/28 financial year.

findings.headline: Added years pension costs of £210,002 from legacy scheme were not budgeted and now create unplanned overspend.
findings.detail: Corporate Financing & Debt Management service is overspending by £210,002 on 'Added years pension costs for legacy scheme, not budgeted'. This represents unfunded or underestimated pension obligation emerging from past discretionary pension awards (likely discretionary added years or early retirement arrangements).
findings.matters: Unbudgeted pension costs indicate incomplete forecasting of legacy scheme liabilities; adds to structural budget pressures and reduces financial headroom.
findings.figures: Unbudgeted pension overspend £210,002
findings.quote: Compensation Pension Payments 210 0 210 Added years pension costs for legacy scheme, not budgeted.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivering only 45% of budget by Q3 with £8.7m being reprofiled into future years.
findings.detail: Capital programme forecast outturn £8.023m against revised budget £17.652m, representing 45% delivery rate. Council proposes to reprofile £8.723m into 2026/27 and future years and remove completed schemes. This is material slippage affecting cash flow and capital delivery plans. Positive side effect: borrowing need reduced from originally estimated £6.446m to £1.8m.
findings.matters: Large capital programme slippage indicates either delivery risk (project delays, permitting issues) or financing constraints; impacts cash position, borrowing requirement, and ability to deliver service capacity investment.
findings.figures: Forecast outturn £8.023m of £17.652m budget (45%); reprofiling £8.723m; borrowing need £1.8m (down from £6.446m estimate)
findings.quote: The forecast outturn for the year is £8.023 million, against the revised estimate of £17.652 million, creating a £9.629 million variance. There are several schemes to be reprofiled into 2026/27 and future years, total value of £8.723 million.

findings.headline: Town centre commercial property portfolio facing £450,000 combined void costs and lease renewal income loss; only partially offset by rates appeal.
findings.detail: Town Centre Investment service forecasting £144,000 overspend driven by £200,000 void service charge costs and £250,000 income shortfall from vacant units and challenging lease renewal negotiations. Partially offset by £314,000 business rates appeal refund, but underlying position shows weak commercial property performance with units remaining vacant and tenants renegotiating downward.
findings.matters: Commercial property holdings in underperforming town centres face tenant weakness, vacancy risk, and potential asset value impairment; income volatility from this source affects revenue sustainability.
findings.figures: Void service charge costs £200k, lease renewal income shortfall £250k; partially offset by rates refund £314k
findings.quote: Town Centre Investment 144 0 144 Overspend on service charge void costs (£200k), and shortfall in income (£250k) due to void units and lease renewals. These shortfalls have been partially offset by a successful backdated business rates appeal, resulting in a refund of £314k

findings.headline: Staffing costs overrunning by £106,580 despite £753,000 vacancy margin built into budget; flagged as 'key risk area'.
findings.detail: The Council budgeted for £753,000 in natural staffing vacancies across the year. Despite this allowance, total staff costs are forecast to overspend by £106,580. Report identifies staffing as 'a key risk area for the Council in the delivery of services' comprising 30% of total expenditure. Specific services showing material overspends include Corporate Financing & Debt Management (£210k), Transformation (£96k), and Property & Economic Development (£93k).
findings.matters: Inability to achieve budgeted vacancy rates despite structured planning indicates either successful recruitment creating unbudgeted cost or control deficiency; staffing is typically largest controllable cost.
findings.figures: Staffing overspend £106,580 (forecast £13.991m v budget £13.884m); vacancy margin assumption £753,000
findings.quote: Staffing equates to 30% of our total expenditure budgets and is a key risk area for the Council in the delivery of services. A £753,000 vacancy margin is assumed within the budget to account for natural vacancies through the year, which is not currently forecast to be met as we are projecting an over spend on staffing costs as shown below:

findings.headline: Planning application income down £610,000 with shortfall attributed to 'general downturn in applications' from economic conditions, repeating last year's position.
findings.detail: Planning income is forecast to undershoot budget by £610,000. Report states this 'is in line with last year's outturn', indicating this is not a one-off variance but a persistent income pressure. Cause given is 'a general downturn in application due to economic conditions' affecting the local development market.
findings.matters: Persistent discretionary income weakness signals reduced local economic activity and development appetite; councils relying on planning/building control income face revenue volatility in downturns.
findings.figures: Planning application income shortfall £610,000
findings.quote: A forecast shortfall in planning application income of £610,000 against budget which Is in line with last year's outturn. There has been a general downturn in application due to economic conditions.

findings.headline: General Fund balance (£0.54m) breached the Council's own CFO-determined minimum requirement of £1.6m by £1.06m.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer has set a requirement that the Council hold £1.6m in General Fund Balance (5-10% of net service expenditure) and £8m in specific earmarked reserves. The Council is now below both thresholds. The General Fund is at one-third of the required level. CFO attributes this to 'budget deficit in the year, and each year in the MTFS' (Medium Term Financial Strategy).
findings.matters: Inadequate working capital creates vulnerability to revenue fluctuations or unexpected costs; persistent breach of CFO-set minimum indicates ongoing structural imbalance rather than one-off pressure.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance £0.54m (CFO minimum £1.6m); Specific earmarked reserves £9.6m (CFO target £8m)
findings.quote: There is no statutory minimum level of reserves, but the CFO has determined that the Council should hold £1.6 million in its General Fund Balance, being 5% to 10% of net service expenditure. In addition, £8 million is appropriate for specific earmarked reserves the Council given their nature and future plans. We are currently below these levels due to the budget deficit in the year, and each year in the MTFS.

findings.headline: Section 151 Officer explicitly states that ongoing use of reserves to balance the budget is unsustainable and transformation savings will not restore financial self-sufficiency.
findings.detail: The CFO tells Councillors they are aware of the structural financial position and mitigation plans (transformation programme). However, these mitigations 'will not return the Council to a position where it does not rely on reserves to balance the budget'. The Council is monitoring its position 'in relation to the LGR timescales' (Local Government Reorganisation), indicating reliance on external restructuring rather than operational fix.
findings.matters: A council dependent on structural use of reserves with no clear path to self-sufficiency presents ongoing debt service and liquidity risk; reliance on LGR (uncertain timing and scope) rather than own operational measures is fragile mitigation.
findings.figures: Forecast use of reserves £5.45m in year; total reserves forecast £17.08m earmarked plus £0.54m general fund
findings.quote: Whilst the use of reserves to fund ongoing revenue expenditure is unsustainable in the medium to long term, Councillors are aware of the financial position and what mitigations have been put in place, in particular the transformation programme. These will not, however, return the Council to a position where it does not rely on reserves to balance the budget, but we are closely monitoring the position in relation to the LGR timescales.

findings.paper_title: Surrey Heath BC 24-25 - Disclaimer of opinion, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Formal audit certification cannot be completed until consolidation returns work is finished and National Audit Office confirms Whole of Government Accounts audit completion.
findings.detail: The auditor states it cannot formally conclude the audit or issue an audit certificate until consolidation returns work is complete and the National Audit Office confirms completion of the Whole of Government Accounts audit for 2024-25. The auditor states this work is not considered to have a material effect on the financial statements.
findings.matters: Delayed formal sign-off of the audit extends the period of uncertainty about the council's verified financial position and defers audit completion.
findings.figures: Year ended 31 March 2025
findings.quote: We cannot formally conclude the audit and issue an audit certificate for Surrey Heath Borough Council for the year ended 31 March 2025 in accordance with the requirements of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 and the Code of Audit Practice until we have completed the work necessary in relation to the Authority's consolidation returns and we have received confirmation from the National Audit Office the audit of the Whole of Government Accounts is complete for the year ended 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Surrey Heath BC 24-25 - Disclaimer of opinion, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Council is significantly reliant on reserves to balance the budget and lacks a finalised transformation plan for sustainable savings.
findings.detail: On 25 November 2025, the auditor identified a significant weakness in the council's arrangements for financial sustainability. The auditor found that the council has significant reliance on reserves to balance the budget each year, and this issue remains unresolved. The auditor has recommended the council finalise and implement a transformation plan that delivers recurrent cash-releasing savings at scale.
findings.matters: Dependence on one-off reserve drawdowns to balance annual budgets indicates structural spending problems and is unsustainable long-term. Lenders need to see permanent revenue solutions, not reliance on reserves.
findings.figures: No specific monetary figures provided for reserve drawdown or savings target
findings.quote: Significant weakness in arrangements for financial sustainability identified. The identification of savings to reduce the significant reliance on reserves to balance the budget each year is still relevant for 2024/25. We recommended the council finalise and implement the transformation plan that delivers recurrent cash releasing savings at scale.

findings.paper_title: Surrey Heath BC 24-25 - Disclaimer of opinion, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Auditor has issued a disclaimer of opinion and cannot audit the 2024-25 financial statements.
findings.detail: The auditor was unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by the 27 February 2026 backstop date to conclude whether the financial statements are free from material misstatement. The auditor concluded that the possible effect of these matters could be both material and pervasive. A disclaimer of opinion is one of the most serious audit outcomes, indicating the financial statements cannot be verified.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the council's financial position cannot be independently verified, making it impossible for lenders to assess true financial health or for the finance director to rely on audited accounts.
findings.figures: Year ended 31 March 2025; backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: We have been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by the backstop date to conclude that the Authority's financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 as a whole are free from material misstatement. We have concluded that the possible effect of these matters on the financial statements could be both material and pervasive.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Surrey Heath BC - Audit Findings Report 2024-25, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: £1.9m commercial property debtors with no clear accounting trail; no internal monitoring of tenant arrears or receipts in advance
findings.detail: The council bills tenants for rent and service charges via managing agents but has no internal systems to reconcile tenant arrears, receipts in advance, or service charge balances. The auditor was unable to obtain clarity on how these should be accounted for or tracked, creating a material risk of misstatement in both income and creditor balances.
findings.matters: Without visibility of tenant arrears and advance receipts, the council cannot reliably measure the true value of its property portfolio income or its debtor position. Bad debt provisions may be incomplete.
findings.figures: £1.9m commercial property rent debtors; £0.1m service charge debtors; total property portfolio generating £9.9m income
findings.quote: At the time of concluding our audit work, we have been unable to gain clarity on the Council's arrangements regarding accounting for tenant arrears at year-end, rents received in advance, service charges, and accounting for cash held by managing agents, including timing and recognition of when funds are transferred to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Surrey Heath BC - Audit Findings Report 2024-25, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Significant weaknesses identified in the council's value-for-money arrangements; auditor not satisfied on economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.detail: The auditor has concluded there is a significant weakness in VFM arrangements and cannot confirm the council has made proper arrangements for securing value for money in its use of resources. This is reported separately in the Auditor's Annual Report.
findings.matters: A significant VFM weakness means the council may not be deploying its resources efficiently or achieving value. This affects the sustainability of service provision and may signal organisational or financial management issues.
findings.figures: Assessed as significant weakness in one of three VFM criteria (economy/efficiency/effectiveness, financial sustainability, governance)
findings.quote: We identified a significant weakness in the Authority's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Surrey Heath BC - Audit Findings Report 2024-25, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: £23.3m prior period adjustment required: Joint Waste Services contract was incorrectly accounted for in prior years
findings.detail: The council had been accounting for the Joint Waste contract with partner councils as principal rather than agent, overstating both income and expenditure by £23.3m. This was only discovered during 2024/25 and required restatement of prior-year comparatives. The council's managing agent oversight failed to catch this.
findings.matters: A £23.3m accounting error in a major service contract shows the council's internal controls and reconciliation processes are weak. This scale of restatement reduces confidence in reported reserves and service cost reporting.
findings.figures: Prior period adjustment £23.3m; gross expenditure and income decrease by £23.3m in 2023/24 comparatives
findings.quote: The Council reviewed its accounting arrangements for the Joint Waste Services contract and concluded that it had been accounting for this incorrectly in prior years, resulting in a prior period adjustment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Surrey Heath BC - Audit Findings Report 2024-25, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: £12.4m of fixed assets were omitted from the register and £2.1m were duplicated, requiring prior period adjustments
findings.detail: A review of the fixed asset register identified 77 assets totalling £12.4m (land £7.8m, buildings £4.5m) that the council owned but had not recorded. Additionally, £2.1m of assets were duplicated, categorised in both property plant and equipment and investment properties concurrently. These errors required restatement of prior periods.
findings.matters: Missing and duplicate assets indicate weak capital accounting controls. These corrections suggest the auditor cannot rely on the council's record of what it owns or its capital position, which feeds into MRP calculations and asset valuation.
findings.figures: £12.4m omitted assets (£7.8m land, £4.5m buildings); £2.1m net book value duplicated assets
findings.quote: The Council identified 77 assets that had previously been excluded from the FAR with a total value of £12.4m (land £7.8m and buildings £4.5m) as at 31st March 2025... the net book value of these duplicated assets within the closing position is £2.1m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Surrey Heath BC - Audit Findings Report 2024-25, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision charged at 1.2% of Capital Financing Requirement, well below 2% benchmark, creating long-term financial sustainability risk
findings.detail: The council is not charging enough to repay its debt. The MRP charge is £2.4m (1.2% of CFR) versus a typical 2% benchmark. The auditor has flagged this as indicating potential under-provision. The council applies 50-year useful economic lives to most assets, which the auditor considers unrealistic.
findings.matters: Under-provisioning for debt repayment pushes costs into future years and increases long-term borrowing obligations. This affects the council's medium-term financial plan and raises questions about the sustainability of current spending levels.
findings.figures: MRP charge 2024/25: £2.4m at 1.2% of CFR; benchmark 2%; Capital Financing Requirement closing £199.4m
findings.quote: The Council's Minimum Revenue Provision Charge continues to be 1.2% of its closing Capital Financing Requirement in the preceding year. We would typically consider a benchmark of 2% within the local government sector. The Council's position indicates potential under-provision and long-term financial sustainability risks.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Surrey Heath BC - Audit Findings Report 2024-25, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: £9.9m commercial property income stream has material unresolved accounting weaknesses and a £1.7m discrepancy
findings.detail: The council cannot reconcile rental income recorded in the general ledger to managing agent reports. Lease incentives adjustment of £1.3m was calculated for only 32 of 241+ business units. Cash collected by agents (e.g. £2.7m retained by one agent in 2024/25) is not regularly reconciled. The auditor was unable to complete testing on this material income.
findings.matters: A £9.9m income stream with incomplete accounting and internal monitoring creates uncertainty over actual cash position and debtor balances. If rental income is misstated, reserves and the general fund balance are unreliable.
findings.figures: £9.9m rental income; £1.7m discrepancy identified; £1.3m lease incentives; £5.3m cash for Square property split £2.6m to council and £2.7m retained
findings.quote: The Council does not appear to have its own internal arrangements to monitor income from commercial properties and perform regular reconciliation of income billed and cash collected and received and expenditure incurred is consistent with the data or information received from managing agents.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Surrey Heath BC - Audit Findings Report 2024-25, 03/02/2026 Audit, Standards and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Auditor will disclaim the 2024/25 accounts and cannot form an opinion on the financial statements
findings.detail: Four years of prior disclaimed audits (2018/19–2022/23) mean the auditor has no assurance over opening balances, which propagates through the current year. Incomplete audit testing on material income streams and accounting weaknesses prevent the auditor from reaching a conclusion. A disclaimer means no audit assurance on the published accounts.
findings.matters: Lenders have no audited financial position for this council. The finance position cannot be verified to a professional standard, making lending decisions or covenant monitoring impossible.
findings.figures: £185m external borrowing; five consecutive years disclaimed (2018/19–2024/25)
findings.quote: Due to the lack of assurance over opening balances, unresolved issues in 2023/24 and the incomplete audit testing this year, a disclaimer of opinion will be issued for 2024/25.

findings.headline: Significant challenges obtaining clean debtor and creditor listings; commercial property balances lack adequate supporting documentation and clear accounting trail
findings.detail: Despite claimed improvements, the Council continues to struggle providing clean year-end debtor and creditor listings. Commercial property rent debtors (£1.9m) and service charges debtors (£0.1m) lack clarity on accounting arrangements and cash timing. Creditors listing (£10.4m) contains unresolved historic balances.
findings.matters: Inability to produce clean, supported debtor/creditor schedules indicates weak financial controls; material balances cannot be fully substantiated by external audit.
findings.figures: Short-term debtors £17.3m; Commercial property rent debtors £1.9m; Service charges debtors £0.1m; Creditors £10.4m
findings.quote: Despite some improvements in debtor working papers and listings provided for certain account balances, obtaining clean listings with only valid year end debtors remains challenging for officers... There is a lack of clarity on the Council's financial governance arrangements for income from investment property and the associated costs.

findings.headline: £2.3m misclassification between long-term and short-term borrowing identified and corrected via prior period adjustment
findings.detail: The auditor's review identified a £2.3m classification error between long-term and short-term borrowing for year ended 31 March 2025, corrected through prior period adjustment.
findings.matters: Misclassification of debt maturity affects covenant compliance and refinancing risk assessment; multiple prior period corrections indicate weak internal controls over debt accounting.
findings.figures: £2.3m misclassification; Long-term borrowing £94m; Short-term borrowing £90m
findings.quote: Our review of borrowings identified a £2.3m classification error between long term and short term borrowing for the year ended 31stMarch 2025. The Council have agreed to amend the error through a prior period adjustment.

findings.headline: 50-year useful economic lives for capital assets appear unrealistic; auditor specifically flags Camberley Town Centre Mall (purchased 2016/17, built 1970s) as concerning example
findings.detail: The Council has adopted 50-year useful economic lives for buildings, land, investment properties and heritage assets. The auditor identifies this as 'a major concern', noting it appears unrealistic given actual asset age. Camberley Town Centre Mall, purchased in 2016/17 but built in the 1970s, exemplifies the issue.
findings.matters: Overstated asset lives result in depressed depreciation charges and inflated asset values; this distorts the council's financial position and may mask the true cost of debt.
findings.figures: 50-year UEL for buildings, land, investment property, heritage assets; Camberley Town Centre Mall purchased 2016/17, built 1970s
findings.quote: A major concern and challenge to management is the adoption of the maximum 50-year useful economic lives (UEL) for most assets financed through borrowing, which appears unrealistic (e.g., Camberley Town Centre Mall purchased in 2016/17 with a 50-year horizon despite being built in the 1970s).

findings.headline: Joint Waste Services accounting restated from principal to agent basis, resulting in £23.3m prior period adjustment to gross income and expenditure
findings.detail: The Council reviewed its accounting for the Joint Waste Services partnership (waste collection contract with Elmbridge, Mole Valley, and Woking). It concluded it had been incorrectly accounting as principal rather than agent, requiring a £23.3m prior period adjustment decreasing both gross expenditure and income for 2023/24.
findings.matters: A £23.3m prior period adjustment signals a material accounting error in how a significant joint venture was treated; indicates gaps in accounting expertise or control.
findings.figures: Prior period adjustment £23.3m (decrease to gross expenditure and income)
findings.quote: The Council reviewed its accounting arrangements for the Joint Waste Services contract and concluded that it had been accounting for this incorrectly in prior years, resulting in a prior period adjustment... In summary, gross expenditure and gross income have decreased by £23.3m.

findings.headline: Fixed Asset Register review identified £12.4m of previously unaccounted assets and £2.1m of duplicated assets requiring material prior period adjustments
findings.detail: The 2024/25 fixed asset review identified 77 assets valued at £12.4m (land £7.8m, buildings £4.5m) that the Council owned but had never recorded in the FAR. Separately, £2.1m of duplicate entries were found classified under both property plant and equipment and investment properties simultaneously. These require prior period adjustments.
findings.matters: Material omissions and duplications indicate significant control failures in capital asset accounting; this is symptomatic of the finance team being 'under strain from staff turnover'.
findings.figures: Omitted assets £12.4m (land £7.8m, buildings £4.5m); Duplicate assets £2.1m correction; 77 omitted assets
findings.quote: The Council identified 77 assets that had previously been excluded from the FAR with a total value of £12.4m (land £7.8m and buildings £4.5m) as at 31st March 2025... In addition, management's review also identified assets that had been duplicated in the FAR, resulting in assets being categorised under both property plant and equipment and investment properties concurrently. The net book value of these duplicated assets within the closing position is £2.1m.

findings.headline: £7.5m commercial property rental income stream has unclear governance and weak accounting controls; external assurance review commissioned but findings not yet fully incorporated
findings.detail: The Council receives approximately £7.5m in rental income managed by external agents. During the audit, the Council informed auditors of an external assurance review underway within the property team with draft findings recently reported. The audit has struggled to understand the accounting trail for year-end debtors, receipts in advance, and managing agent cash timing. This work remains in progress.
findings.matters: £7.5m is a material income stream; unclear governance and inability to obtain clean records suggest internal control weaknesses; that management commissioned their own external review indicates they identified concerns.
findings.figures: Rental income £7.5m; Commercial property rent debtors £1.9m; Service charges debtors £0.1m
findings.quote: The Council has approximately £7.5m of rental income disclosed in the accounts. The Council uses managing agents to undertake the billing of income and to oversee the property related expenditure on those properties... Our audit work on the testing of the completeness and accuracy of the accounting for property income is on-going. As a material income stream there is a risk of material misstatement.

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision at only 1.2% of Capital Financing Requirement versus benchmark of 2%, indicating potential under-provision and long-term sustainability risks
findings.detail: The Council's 2024/25 MRP charge is £2.4m (1.2% of £200m CFR), unchanged from prior year. The auditor considers the benchmark to be 2% within the local government sector and explicitly notes this position 'indicates potential under-provision and long-term financial sustainability risks'.
findings.matters: Under-provision of MRP means the council is not setting aside sufficient funds to repay debt in line with asset useful lives, creating medium-term refinancing risk.
findings.figures: MRP charge £2.4m; CFR £200m; Current rate 1.2%; Benchmark 2%; External borrowing £179-185m
findings.quote: The Council's Minimum Revenue Provision Charge continues to be 1.2% of its closing Capital Financing Requirement in the preceding year. We would typically consider a benchmark of 2% within the local government sector. The Council's position indicates potential under-provision and long-term financial sustainability risks.

findings.headline: Auditor will disclaim opinion on 2024/25 accounts due to lack of assurance over opening balances stemming from prior years' disclaimed audits
findings.detail: The auditor has concluded they cannot form an unmodified audit opinion and will issue a disclaimer. This follows four years of disclaimed (unaudited) accounts and the backstop legislation. The lack of assurance over opening balances from the disclaimed 2023/24 audit means they cannot form an opinion on 2024/25.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means no independent verification of financial statements; lenders cannot rely on external audit attestation of financial position.
findings.figures: Four prior years of disclaimed accounts (2018/19 to 2022/23); backstop date 28 February 2026
findings.quote: Owing to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous years' audits were subject to backstop-related disclaimed audit opinions, we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 28 February 2026.

news_drafts.lead: A sudden reduction in an asset's useful life and reclassification away from investment property suggests concerns about the asset's performance, cash-generative ability, or long-term viability. This may signal underlying operational or market pressures on…

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme severely underspent: only £5.346m spent against £17.474m budgeted (69% slippage).
news_drafts.lead: Repeated significant capital slippage suggests poor forecasting, planning difficulties, or constrained project delivery capacity. This affects the council's ability to maintain assets and execute planned service improvements.
